### `sell_price`

What one unit of this product sells for. Where it is unset the engine uses the demand-weighted mean of the outbound arcs' prices, which is usually what the user means and is why leaving it blank is not an error.

**The engine calls this `required`.** Revenue and lost-sales valuation — the terminal default of 1.0 makes revenue KPIs meaningless.

**Resolution** — how a value is decided when more than one source could supply one.

| | |
|---|---|
| Default mode | `asserted` |

hybrid is NULL because scsim has nowhere to put a spread: cost and unit_price are bare floats on Material and Product, with no distribution, no CV and no sampling path anywhere in the engine. Recording `hybrid: null` here is a statement about the ENGINE, not about the world — prices obviously vary. Giving them a spread is an engine change on the scsim track; see the RFC in PLAN.md §14. Do not invent one in this contract: a contract that describes a capability the engine does not have is how a fallback ends up in code with no contract entry, which is what I6 forbids in the other direction. As with materials.cost, the demand-weighted outbound mean is a visible substitution, not an estimate.

> D21 in one line: the user types `sell_price`, the database column is `sell_price`, and the engine's field is `unit_price`. The legacy docs led with the engine's name, so a reader searching their own CSV for `unit_price` found nothing. The manual leads with `sell_price`.

### `production_capacity`

How much of this product the plant can make per week. The canonical G4 example: when it is unset the engine invents a capacity generous enough that capacity never binds, so an unset value silently turns off the constraint the user thinks they are simulating.

| | |
|---|---|
| Type | `numeric` |
| Grain | `rate` |
| Unit | `units per week` — fixed |
| Added by | `20260614000001_item_master.sql` |
| Read by the engine | `project_map.py::_map_products -> Product.production_capacity` |
| Transform | float() when > 0 |
| When NULL, the engine uses | max(2 x demand, 1000) — a value chosen so the constraint never binds |
| Validated at ingest | numeric > 0 |
| Rendered at | *not yet recorded (WP 5.1)* |

**The engine calls this `recommended`.** With no capacity source the engine defaults to max(2·demand, 1000), so plant capacity never binds.

Fallback chain, from the engine's own registry: production_policy_capacity (info) → twice_demand_floor_1000 (warn).

|---|---|---|---|

**Resolution** — how a value is decided when more than one source could supply one.

| | |
|---|---|
| Default mode | `asserted` |
| Assertable by | `csv_upload`, `item_master_form` |
| Estimable from | **never** — this value may not be estimated |
| Hybrid (centre / spread) | **none** — the engine has no variability field for this quantity |
| On conflict | `assertion_wins` |

estimable_from is EMPTY and that is a positive statement, not an omission. This is an engineering or commercial fact that someone knows exactly — it is written on a drawing, in a contract, or on a machine's nameplate. Fitting a distribution to it would produce a number with error bars around something that has no error, and the error bars would be believed. A future estimator reading this contract must refuse this field. This is the canonical G4 field: unset, the engine invents max(2 x demand, 1000), which is chosen so the constraint never binds. Estimating it from output would do the same thing with more ceremony — output is bounded by demand, so the fitted capacity can never explain a shortage.

**Resolution** — how a value is decided when more than one source could supply one.

| | |
|---|---|
| Default mode | `hybrid` |
| Assertable by | `csv_upload`, `item_master_form` |
| Estimable from | `outbound_logistics.volume (weekly-normalized)` |
| Hybrid (centre / spread) | `products.demand_mean` / `products.demand_cv + products.demand_min/demand_max` |
| On conflict | `assertion_wins` |

default_mode is `hybrid` and this is the only field in the twelve where that is true. Demand is the one quantity here that is genuinely observed rather than specified: the user may state a figure, and the outbound arcs independently say what was actually taken. The engine already resolves it that way — the master value wins, the weekly-normalized outbound volume stands in when it is unset. on_conflict is assertion_wins: a stated forecast beats history, because a forecast is a decision about the future and history is not.

> D21: CSV header `demand_mean`, engine field `demand_mode`. The rename is not cosmetic — calling a mode a mean is a modelling claim. Both recorded.
